title: Your Fuel Table Was Built for $3.66 Diesel: FSC Decisions Before Winter 2026
summary: Diesel hit $6.28 on Oct 19, 2026, up $2.66 in a year, with distillate stocks tight. Where FSC pegs, lag, PADD spreads, and deadhead leak margin.
body_markdown:
On Monday, March 2, 2026, the weekly federal diesel survey put the U.S. on-highway average at $3.897 a gallon. One week later it read $4.859. That 96.2 cent move is the largest single-week jump in the weekly series, which runs back to 1994. A shop billing fuel off the prior month's average spent March invoicing against February's number (about $3.72) while its drivers paid a March average closer to $4.92. Nobody broke a rule. The table did exactly what it was written to do.


That is the problem heading into winter. In this morning's release (October 20, 2026, reflecting Monday, October 19 prices), the national average was $6.276, up 9.7 cents on the week and $2.656 above a year earlier. It was the first weekly increase after three straight declines. The record of $6.529 was set on September 21, 2026, well above the June 20, 2022 high of $5.810. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) expects retail distillate to stay above $6 in October and ease only gradually. Most fuel surcharge programs in North American trucking were calibrated in a calmer regime. The 2025 weekly average was roughly $3.66, and a national ops-cost benchmark described 2025 as diesel's most stable year since the pandemic, with only 41 cents between the high and low. Winter 2026 is where tables built for that world start leaking.


## The regime changed. The tables did not.


The national ops-cost benchmark (2026 update, covering 2025 operations) put fuel at $0.482 per mile, essentially flat with 2024, on fleet fuel economy of 7.43 MPG. Its Q1 2026 indicators already showed fuel cost per mile up 5.9%, and that was before the September run-up.


Run the same 7.43 MPG against the October 19 national average and fuel cost is about 84 cents per mile at retail. That is roughly 36 cents per mile above the 2025 benchmark on a single line item, on freight that was often priced, contracted, or bid when diesel looked boring.


The FSC is supposed to absorb that swing. Whether it does depends on five design choices most shops have not revisited in years: the base peg, the MPG divisor, the index and its timing, the mileage source, and the pass-through rules between carrier, broker, and shipper.


## Winter makes the distillate math worse


Diesel and heating oil are the same distillate pool, and that pool is short.


-


**National stocks:** EIA's weekly petroleum data showed U.S. distillate inventories at 102.6 million barrels for the week ending October 9, 2026, down 2.5 million barrels on the week and 12.3% below the same week of 2025.


-


**East Coast stocks:** PADD 1 distillate stood at 21.5 million barrels, 22.3% below a year earlier. New England was down 40.7% and the Central Atlantic down 32.9%.


-


**The forecast:** EIA's October 6, 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook said East Coast inventories were 32% below their five-year seasonal average in September and are expected to stay 20% to 30% below average through the winter. It forecasts retail diesel averaging $5.19 for 2026 and $4.49 for 2027, with crack spreads staying high relative to history.


-


**Exports pulling barrels away:** EIA's Winter Fuels Outlook (published October 6 and summarized October 7) said U.S. distillate exports rose 20% in the first seven months of 2026, with heating oil prices forecast 34% above last winter and national distillate stocks about 11% below the five-year average in Q4 2026.


-


**Hauling capacity stretched:** FMCSA amended its hours-of-service waiver for gasoline and diesel transport on October 15, 2026, running September 16 through December 16, 2026, citing global supply disruptions.


One line in the STEO matters more to FSC design than any headline price: EIA expects that decreases in wholesale crack spreads "will not immediately translate into lower retail prices," because retail and distribution margins were compressed in 2026 and should rebuild in 2027. Read that as a warning. The pump may fall more slowly than the futures, and your index tracks the pump.


## Where the margin actually leaks


### 1. Index timing and lag


EIA collects the cash self-serve on-highway diesel price, taxes included, as of 8:00 a.m. local time each Monday, and publishes around 10:00 a.m. ET Tuesday. When a federal holiday lands on Monday, it publishes Wednesday instead (October 12 data, collected on Columbus Day, came out October 14). Your program then adds its own lag. Which week applies: tender date, ship date, or delivery date? Weekly or monthly average? Prior week or current week?


Every extra day of lag is a loan. On the way up, the carrier lends to the shipper. On the way down, the shipper lends to the carrier. The March 2026 example (February average billed against March pump prices) shows the size: roughly $1.14 per gallon, or about 15 cents per mile at 7.43 MPG, for weeks.


A second gap sits under the index itself. EIA reports a retail cash price. Many fleets buy below it through discounted network pricing. That spread is real money, and it changes when retail margins move, which EIA says they will in 2027.


### 2. Regional PADD spreads


The October 19 national average was $6.276. Regional readings ran from $5.740 in the Lower Atlantic and $5.903 on the Gulf Coast to $6.508 in the Central Atlantic, $7.394 on the West Coast, and $8.242 in California. That is a $2.34 spread between California and the Gulf Coast in the same week. The West Coast also rose fastest, up 15.4 cents on the week against 9.7 cents nationally.


A national index on a California-heavy dedicated lane under-recovers by about $1.97 per gallon against the state reading, roughly 26 cents per mile at 7.43 MPG. A national index on Gulf Coast or Southeast freight over-recovers, and a sharp procurement analyst will eventually notice.


Taxes are part of the spread and they move on their own calendar. California's diesel excise rose from 46.6 to 48.2 cents per gallon on July 1, 2026, with a 13% sales tax rate on diesel (plus district taxes) for July 2026 through June 2027. Its IFTA rate is 97.9 cents per gallon. Pennsylvania's oil company franchise tax on undyed diesel is 74.1 cents for calendar 2026, and the Department of Revenue announces the 2027 rate by December 15 based on average wholesale prices. The federal diesel excise remains 24.4 cents.


### 3. The MPG divisor and the base peg


Most FSC tables reduce to one formula: (index minus peg) divided by an assumed MPG, per mile. Both inputs are policy choices, not facts.


For illustration only: with a $1.25 peg and a 6 MPG divisor, $6.276 diesel yields about 84 cents per mile. The same peg at 7.43 MPG yields about 68 cents. The 16 cent gap grows as diesel rises, so a divisor that looked harmless at $3.66 becomes a negotiating flashpoint at $6. Equipment and weight matter. The benchmark showed 7.56 MPG at 60,001 to 70,000 lbs. operating weight but 6.20 MPG above 80,000 lbs. One divisor across dry van, heavy flatbed, and reefer is a guess that is wrong in both directions.


### 4. Reefer unit fuel


Most tables price tractor miles. Reefer units burn fuel while the truck sits. The benchmark found average dwell time for refrigerated and flatbed fleets above the two-hour detention threshold in 2025. If your reefer fuel is not a separate line, or a separate table based on hours, it is buried in linehaul that was priced before September. Measure your own unit burn from telematics or fuel tickets. Do not borrow someone else's gallons per hour.


### 5. Deadhead and the mileage source


FSC is typically billed on loaded, rated miles. Trucks burn on all miles. The benchmark put non-tank deadhead at 16.5% in 2025 and tank deadhead at 44.3%. At 84 cents per mile retail fuel, every unrecovered empty mile costs more than it did a year ago. The mileage source matters too. If the rate con uses shortest-route miles and the truck runs practical-route miles, the FSC is short on every load before the index even prints.


### 6. Broker all-in versus carrier FSC


Brokers carry the sharpest timing risk. Carriers quote spot all-in and reprice fuel instantly. Contract shippers pay linehaul plus a lagged FSC. In a rising market, buy rates jump this week while sell-side fuel catches up next week or next month. In a falling market the cushion reverses, but only if the shipper contract does not reset first.


## Asset, broker, and hybrid: the decisions differ


**Asset carriers** own the burn. The priority is matching the table to how you actually consume fuel. That means regional or state indexes on concentrated lanes, divisors by equipment and weight band, a reefer fuel line, and a written position on deadhead recovery for dedicated work.


**Brokers** own the timing gap. Decide which index week applies to each load, align buy-side and sell-side effective dates, and put a defined window on all-in spot quotes, since a quote that sits through an EIA release is a price you no longer control.


**Hybrids** need both, plus a rule for when brokered cover finishes a move that started on a company truck. The FSC billed to the shipper should not change because the asset changed.


## Bid season 2027: do not bake $6 diesel into linehaul


RFPs being built now will run into a year EIA expects to average $4.49 diesel. If fuel gets folded into all-in linehaul at today's prices, the shipper overpays as diesel falls and will reopen the contract. If the peg resets with no floor language, a falling market can produce a near-zero or negative surcharge nobody planned for.


The defensible position is clean separation. Price linehaul as linehaul. Set the peg and divisor with a stated rationale. Name the index, the region, the week, and the effective-date rule in the contract. Then the 2027 decline flows through the FSC instead of through a rate dispute in the middle of the term.


## Encode the program, do not remember it


Every freight business burns, buys, and resells fuel differently. A grocery reefer fleet, a heavy-haul flatbed shop, and a brokerage covering Gulf Coast dry van should not share one table. The serious operators encode that uniqueness in the system that rates, bills, and settles:


-


**FSC tables per customer and per equipment type** , each with its own peg, divisor, index (national, PADD, or state), and effective-date rule.


-


**Index-week logic** that stamps the applicable EIA week on every load at tender, so billing and settlement use the same number.


-


**Separate accessorial lines** for reefer fuel and recoverable deadhead, with contract terms attached.


-


**Permissioned overrides** with reason codes, so sales cannot waive fuel on a lane without a record.


-


**Margin alerts** when buy-side all-in fuel exposure outruns sell-side FSC on a load or lane.


When those rules match how your shop really runs, a 96 cent week becomes a report, not a quarter-end surprise.


## What to do this week


-


Pull every active FSC table. Record peg, divisor, index, region, update cadence, and effective-date rule.


-


Re-price your top 20 lanes at the October 19 regional readings, not the national average.


-


Flag every contract where the divisor or peg has no written rationale.


-


Measure reefer unit fuel and deadhead recovery on your largest accounts.


-


For brokerage desks, align buy and sell index weeks and put an expiry on all-in spot quotes.


-


Put December 15 (Pennsylvania's 2027 rate notice) and the November 10, 2026 STEO on the billing calendar.


-


Draft 2027 RFP language that separates linehaul from fuel and states floor terms.


## FAQ


### What was the U.S. on-highway diesel average on October 19, 2026?


EIA's weekly survey put it at $6.276 per gallon (released October 20), up $2.656 from a year earlier and below the record $6.529 set September 21, 2026.


### Why do fuel surcharges lag actual pump costs?


Because the index is weekly, published a day or two after collection, and many programs add a further lag by using a prior week or prior month average. In March 2026, a one-week jump of 96.2 cents showed how large that gap can get.


### Should we use a national or regional diesel index?


Use a regional or state index on concentrated lanes. On October 19, 2026, California read $8.242 while the Gulf Coast read $5.903, so a national index misprices both.


### Will diesel be lower in 2027?


EIA's October 6, 2026 outlook forecasts retail diesel averaging $4.49 in 2027 versus $5.19 in 2026, but expects distillate inventories to stay below average and retail prices to fall more slowly than wholesale.


### Should reefer unit fuel be part of the FSC?


It should be recovered somewhere explicit, either as a separate hours-based line or a separate table, because tractor-mile tables do not capture fuel burned while the unit runs at the dock.


### What should 2027 RFP fuel language include?


At minimum, a named index and region, the applicable index week, the effective-date rule (tender, ship, or delivery), the peg and divisor with rationale, and floor terms for a falling market.
